title: What is law?
subtitle: Framing the question jurisprudence asks
objectives: Explain why jurisprudence treats 'what is law?' as a genuine, unsettled question rather than something a statute book already answers
Distinguish a descriptive (analytical) claim about law from a normative claim about law, and classify a given statement as one or the other
Use law, morality and convention as a rough starting map to classify a social rule, and identify what remains contestable about that classification

leadingAuthorities.citation: Hart, The Concept of Law (1961), ch. 1
leadingAuthorities.role: Frames 'what is law?' as a genuinely persistent, contested question and sets out the recurring puzzles the rest of the book answers
Reframes the question around law's distinctive claim to legitimate authority over those it governs

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: This is a framing lesson, not a verdict. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this brief note appears: 'You can define the terms — this lesson checks whether you can tell a descriptive claim from a normative one when they're dressed up as the same sentence.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on recall here before. The test pool below leans on classification: expect scenarios and short extracts, not bare definitions.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and take it slowly — the descriptive/normative distinction is the tool every later lesson in this module assumes you already have.

overview.hook: Ask a solicitor 'what's the law on unfair dismissal' and you'll have an answer, with citations, inside five minutes. Ask a jurisprudence scholar 'what is law?' and you could occupy them for the rest of their career — and get a different answer from the scholar in the next office. This module doesn't resolve that disagreement. It teaches you to state, attack and defend each side of it, starting here with what the question even means.

parts.heading: A question lawyers don't usually have to ask
parts.voice: argumentative — states why the question is harder than it looks
body: Practising lawyers spend their careers answering questions of the form 'what does the law require here?' — a factual, researchable question, answered by finding the relevant statute, case or regulation and applying it. Jurisprudence asks a different, prior question: what makes something count as law at all, as opposed to a moral rule, a social custom, or simply an order backed by a threat?

The two questions look similar because they share a word, but they sit at different levels. The first assumes we already know what law is and asks about its content. The second asks what the word 'law' is even picking out — why a Act of Parliament binds you but a supermarket's dress code, or a gang boss's demand for money, does not (or does it? — that comparison is exactly the kind of puzzle this module spends fifteen lessons taking seriously).

Hart opened The Concept of Law by observing how strange it is that a question this basic remains this contested: serious thinkers have offered diverse, and sometimes deliberately paradoxical, answers to 'what is law?' for as long as the question has been asked. That persistence is not a sign the question is badly formed. It is a sign that several rival, carefully reasoned answers are genuinely available — and a competent lawyer should be able to set out each of them fairly, not just recite the one they personally favour.

components.definition: The study of the nature of law itself — what law is, what makes it binding, and how it relates to morality and social order — as distinct from the study of what any particular legal rule provides.

interaction.prompt: A first-year student says: 'Jurisprudence is just an abstract way of asking what the law says on a topic.' Is that an accurate description of the question this module is about?
options: No — jurisprudence asks what makes something count as law at all, not what a particular law provides
Yes — jurisprudence and legal research are the same activity at a higher level of generality
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. Legal research assumes the category 'law' is settled and looks for content within it; jurisprudence interrogates the category itself.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Not quite — legal research already assumes we know what counts as law and goes looking for its content. Jurisprudence asks the prior question of what makes anything count as law in the first place.

parts.heading: Two questions wearing one name: descriptive and normative jurisprudence
parts.voice: structural — a distinction students will return to throughout the module
body: Almost every theory in this module can be sorted, roughly, by which of two questions it is primarily trying to answer — and mixing the two up is the single most common source of confused essays in this area.

A descriptive (or analytical) claim about law tries to give an accurate account of what law actually is, as a matter of social fact — how legal systems in fact operate, what in fact makes a rule count as legally valid within a given system — without saying whether that content is good or bad. A normative claim about law is a piece of moral or political philosophy directed at law: what the law ought to require, whether an existing rule is just, or whether it deserves obedience.

The two questions can point to different answers about the very same rule. A strict descriptive theorist can accurately describe a deeply unjust statute as 'valid law' within its system, precisely because validity is being used as a social-fact concept. A normative theorist may deny that an unjust 'law' is really law at all, or insist that even if it is law, it does not bind anyone in conscience. Neither move is confused — they are answering different questions. Keeping the two apart, without assuming one side has already won, is the discipline this whole module asks of you.

components.label: Descriptive vs normative jurisprudence
points: Descriptive (analytical) jurisprudence: what is law, as a matter of social fact? An account of how legal systems actually work, offered without a verdict on whether their content is good.
Normative jurisprudence: what should the law be, or what makes it deserve obedience? A piece of moral/political philosophy aimed at law.
The same rule can get different answers on each question — a theorist can call a rule 'valid law' descriptively while denying, normatively, that it deserves to be obeyed.

interaction.prompt: Tap the sentence below that is making a normative claim, not a descriptive one.
interaction.scenarioText: In System X, officials in fact treat a rule enacted by the legislature as legally valid, regardless of its content. A rule enacted through that same process, however, does not deserve obedience if it seriously violates basic justice, whatever officials happen to think of it.
tappableSpans: as legally valid, regardless of its content
does not deserve obedience if it seriously violates basic justice
whatever officials happen to think of it
interaction.correctSpan: does not deserve obedience if it seriously violates basic justice
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. That clause isn't describing what officials do — it's asserting a moral conclusion about what should count as binding, independent of official practice. That's the signature of a normative claim.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the clause that goes beyond describing what officials actually do or accept, and instead asserts what ought to bind people regardless of official practice — that shift from 'is' to 'ought' marks the normative claim.

parts.heading: A rough map: law, morality, convention
parts.voice: worked-example — builds the map through contrasting cases before naming the categories
body: Before the module gets into rival theories of law, it's worth having a rough starting map of three overlapping-but-distinct categories: law, morality, and mere social convention. None of the theories in this module accept this map as the final word — several exist specifically to complicate or reject parts of it — but it's a usable first cut.

Failing to pay a debt you owe under a contract is (in most systems) both a legal wrong, enforceable through courts, and something most people would also call a moral failing. Committing murder is legal and moral wrongdoing at once, which is why it's such a poor example for testing whether law and morality are really separate — almost every theory agrees on that case. Failing to send a thank-you note after a dinner party is neither: no court will hear the claim, and most people would call it a lapse of manners rather than of morals — a pure social convention.

The genuinely interesting cases sit in the gaps. Queue-jumping is a convention with no legal force in England and Wales, but many people feel it as a moral wrong, not just a rude one. A statutory duty to wear a seatbelt is unambiguously legal, but plenty of people don't feel any independent moral pull towards it at all — for them it's a rule they follow only because it's law. The map doesn't dissolve these disputes; it gives you vocabulary to state exactly where a given disagreement sits.

components.title: A first-cut classification: law, morality or convention?
components.description: A rough decision path for placing a social rule on the starting map this lesson uses — not a settled theory, but a tool for spotting what a dispute is actually about.

nodes.label: Is the rule enforced (or enforceable) through state institutions claiming ultimate authority — courts, legislatures, police?
Yes → provisionally 'legal' on this map, whether or not it is also widely felt to be moral
No → is the rule felt to bind regardless of institutions, such that breaking it is wrongdoing rather than mere impoliteness?
No → provisionally a mere social convention — breach carries social cost, not a felt sense of wrongdoing

components.textAlternative: To place a rule on this rough map: first ask whether it is enforced or enforceable through state institutions claiming ultimate authority. If so, it is provisionally 'legal', whether or not it is also widely felt to be moral. If not, ask whether the rule is felt to bind regardless of institutions, such that breaking it counts as wrongdoing rather than mere impoliteness — if so, it is provisionally 'moral'. If neither applies, it is provisionally a mere social convention, whose breach carries social cost but no felt sense of wrongdoing.

interaction.prompt: Using this lesson's rough map, which scenario describes a rule that is legal rather than merely conventional?
interaction.scenarioA: Failing to send a thank-you card after being a guest at a dinner party
interaction.scenarioB: Failing to file and pay income tax on time, resulting in HMRC penalties
interaction.explanation: B is enforced through state institutions with a claim to ultimate authority — HMRC and, if it escalates, the courts — so it lands on the 'legal' side of the map. A carries only social cost, with no institutional enforcement and (for most people) no felt sense of wrongdoing, so it sits as a mere convention.

parts.heading: Three puzzles any theory of law has to answer
parts.voice: structural — a reference-style part previewing the module's shape
body: Hart's opening chapter identifies, in different words, three recurring puzzles that any serious theory of law has to say something about — and this module is organised, loosely, around rival answers to them.

First: how does a legal obligation differ from simply being forced to comply, as when a gunman orders you to hand over your wallet? Both involve a threat and a demand for compliance, yet we describe only one as creating an 'obligation'. Second: is there a necessary connection between law and morality, or are the two entirely separate systems that happen to overlap in content most of the time? Third: what exactly is a 'rule', and how far can an entire legal system be explained as a system of rules, as opposed to something looser — principles, policies, official practice, raw power?

You'll meet direct answers to all three across this module: the command theory's attempt (and failure) to answer the first without more than threats and habits; Hart's own answer built on primary and secondary rules; the Hart–Fuller debate fought almost entirely over the second; and Dworkin's challenge to whether 'rules' can carry the third question's weight at all. For now, just hold the three puzzles in mind as the questions everything else in this module is trying to answer.

components.label: Hart's three recurring puzzles
points: How does a legal obligation differ from simply being coerced, as by a gunman's threat?
Is there a necessary connection between law and morality, or are they entirely separate systems?
What is a 'rule', and how far can a legal system be explained as a system of rules at all?

interaction.prompt: Put these three puzzles in the order this lesson introduces them.
items: How does legal obligation differ from being coerced, as by a gunman?
Is there a necessary connection between law and morality?
What is a 'rule', and can law be explained as a system of rules?
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the order this lesson raises them in — and roughly the order the module tackles them, from the command theory through the Hart–Fuller debate to Dworkin's challenge to the rule-based picture itself.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Check the order against the lesson text: the gunman puzzle comes first, the law/morality connection second, and the nature of 'rules' themselves third.

parts.heading: Raz: law's claim to authority
parts.voice: reflective — closes the lesson by widening the frame
body: Raz's The Authority of Law approaches 'what is law?' from a slightly different angle to Hart's: rather than starting from rules, Raz starts from the observation that legal systems characteristically claim to have legitimate authority over the people subject to them — law doesn't just try to influence behaviour, the way advice or a threat does, it claims the right to be obeyed simply because it is law, independent of whether its content is otherwise persuasive.

This reframing matters because it gives a second, independent reason to keep the descriptive and normative questions separate. You can ask, descriptively, what it takes for a system to count as making this kind of authority claim (a question about the structure of legal systems as social institutions) without yet asking, normatively, whether any given legal system's claim to authority is actually justified. Raz's own answer to the second question — his 'service conception' of authority — sits beyond this module's core spine, but the framing is worth carrying forward: much of the rest of this module is, one way or another, an argument about what law's claim to authority rests on, and whether it can be made good.
Keep both puzzles — Hart's three, and Raz's authority claim — loosely in mind as you move into the next two lessons, which begin the module's oldest and most persistent rival answer: natural law.

components.definition: Raz's observation that legal systems characteristically claim the right to be obeyed simply because they are law, not merely because their content happens to be persuasive — a claim that can be examined descriptively (what does making this claim require?) separately from normatively (is any given claim actually justified?).

interaction.prompt: How confident are you that 'what is law?' and 'what does the law require on this specific point?' are the same question, just phrased at different levels of generality?
sliderLabels: Two fundamentally different kinds of question
interaction.correctPosition: Two fundamentally different kinds of question
interaction.explanation: They're different in kind, not just in scope. 'What does the law require here?' presupposes an answer to 'what is law?' and searches within it; 'what is law?' asks what makes anything count as law at all — a question legal research tools cannot answer for you.

testPool.prompt: State the difference between a descriptive (analytical) claim about law and a normative claim about law.
acceptableAnswers: descriptive describes what law is as a fact, normative says what law ought to be
descriptive is factual, normative is moral/evaluative
testPool.modelAnswer: A descriptive claim tries to give an accurate account of what law actually is, as a matter of social fact, without judging its content. A normative claim asserts what the law ought to be, or whether it deserves obedience — a piece of moral or political philosophy directed at law.

testPool.prompt: Name the three recurring puzzles Hart identifies at the start of The Concept of Law as central to 'what is law?'
acceptableAnswers: obligation vs coercion, law and morality's connection, the nature of rules
gunman puzzle, law/morality connection, what is a rule
testPool.modelAnswer: How legal obligation differs from mere coercion (the gunman case); whether there is a necessary connection between law and morality; and what a 'rule' is, and how far law can be explained as a system of rules.

testPool.prompt: Raz's The Authority of Law reframes 'what is law?' chiefly around law's claim to what?
options: Legitimate authority over those it governs
Popularity with the general public

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the three categories in this lesson's starting law/morality/convention map?
options: Law
Morality
Convention
A free-standing category for professional codes of etiquette
testPool.trapExplanation: The map is deliberately a rough, three-way starting point, not an exhaustive taxonomy. A professional code of etiquette is simply a species of convention (or, where it also carries a felt sense of wrongdoing, morality) — not a fourth category in its own right.

testPool.prompt: A student writes: 'Jurisprudence assumes there's one correct answer to what law is, and every theory is competing to find it.' What's wrong with this, given how this module frames the subject?
options: Nothing — that is an accurate description of the module
The module treats rival theories as defensible, competing positions to be stated, attacked and defended fairly, not as a race towards one settled correct answer
Jurisprudence contains no theories at all, only case law
testPool.trapExplanation: The student's framing smuggles in exactly the assumption this module avoids. There is no examiner's mark scheme declaring one school correct; the skill being tested throughout is accurate, non-partisan statement of each position, not adopting one.

testPool.prompt: In the passage below, highlight the sentence that expresses a normative claim rather than a descriptive one.
testPool.passage: In this legal system, courts in fact recognise a statute passed by the legislature as valid law, and apply it accordingly, regardless of its content. Even so, a statute of this kind does not deserve the citizen's obedience if it demands something seriously unjust, whatever the courts happen to do with it.
testPool.ratioSentence: Even so, a statute of this kind does not deserve the citizen's obedience if it demands something seriously unjust, whatever the courts happen to do with it.

testPool.prompt: In the passage below, highlight the sentence that best captures Raz's idea of law's 'claim to authority'.
testPool.passage: Advice tries to persuade you by the strength of its content; a threat tries to move you by fear of a consequence. Law is different again: it presents itself as binding simply because it is law, claiming the right to be obeyed independently of whether you find its content persuasive on the merits. Whether any given legal system's claim of this kind is actually justified is a separate question again.
testPool.ratioSentence: Law is different again: it presents itself as binding simply because it is law, claiming the right to be obeyed independently of whether you find its content persuasive on the merits.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact in this scenario that places the rule on the 'legal' side of this lesson's starting map, rather than the 'convention' side.
testPool.scenarioText: Residents of a shared building have an unwritten understanding not to play loud music after 11pm. One night a resident ignores this, and the following week the building's freeholder issues a formal breach notice under the lease, with the threat of forfeiture proceedings in court if it happens again.
tappableSpans: issues a formal breach notice under the lease
threat of forfeiture proceedings in court
testPool.correctSpan: threat of forfeiture proceedings in court
testPool.feedbackCorrect: Right. Once a state institution — the court, via forfeiture proceedings — stands behind enforcement, the rule (as embodied in the lease term) sits on the legal side of the map, even though it started life looking like a mere social understanding.
testPool.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the moment state enforcement enters the picture, rather than the informal understanding itself. An unwritten norm only crosses onto the 'legal' side of this map once an institution like a court stands ready to enforce it.

testPool.prompt: Order the steps this lesson suggests for classifying a claim about law as descriptive or normative.
items: Identify what the claim asserts — a fact about official or institutional practice, or a value judgement about what should happen
Check whether the claim could be true even if the practice it describes were widely regarded as unjust
If it could still be true, classify it as descriptive; if its truth depends on the practice being justified, classify it as normative

testPool.prompt: Which scholar's claim below is descriptive rather than normative?
testPool.scenarioA: 'Officials in System Y in fact treat a rule enacted through the standard legislative procedure as legally valid, whatever its moral content.'
testPool.scenarioB: 'A rule enacted through System Y's standard legislative procedure ought not to be treated as valid if it seriously offends basic justice.'
testPool.explanation: A reports what officials in fact do and accept — a claim about social practice that could be true even of a deeply unjust system. B asserts what officials ought to do, independent of what they in fact accept — a normative claim.

testPool.prompt: In the extract below from a hypothetical jurisprudence essay, which sentence is doing normative work — asserting what should be the case, rather than reporting what is the case?
options: 'Legal officials in most developed systems treat a settled rule of recognition as the ultimate test of validity.'
'A rule of recognition of this kind deserves the loyalty of citizens only if the system it identifies as law is minimally just.'
'Rules of recognition vary considerably between common law and civil law systems.'
testPool.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Only this sentence moves from describing a social practice to asserting a condition that practice must meet to deserve loyalty — the marker of a normative claim.
testPool.feedbackIncorrect: The other two sentences report what officials do or how systems vary — pure description. Only the sentence about what a rule of recognition 'deserves' is making a normative claim.

testPool.prompt: A small community enforces 'no eating in the shrine' purely through communal disapproval and exclusion from social events — there is no court, police force or formal institution involved at any point. Using this lesson's starting map, how should the rule be classified?
options: Provisionally legal, because it is a rule people take seriously
Provisionally moral or conventional, because there is no institutional enforcement of the kind the map requires for 'legal'
It cannot be classified — the map only applies to written rules
testPool.explanation: With no state or state-like institution enforcing it, the rule fails the first branch of the map's decision path. Whether it then counts as 'moral' or merely 'conventional' depends on whether breach is felt as wrongdoing or merely as impoliteness — but either way, it is not 'legal' on this map.

testPool.prompt: In State Z, courts consistently treat a directive as legally valid and enforce it, even though independent observers widely regard its content as unjust. Does resolving the descriptive question ('is this directive law in State Z?') automatically resolve the normative question ('should the directive be obeyed?')?
options: No — descriptively answering that it is valid law leaves entirely open whether it deserves obedience; that is a separate, normative inquiry
Yes — once something is shown to be valid law, it automatically follows that it should be obeyed
The two questions are identical, so there is nothing further to ask
testPool.explanation: This is exactly the gap this lesson is built to preserve. A directive can be descriptively valid law in State Z (a social fact about how its officials operate) while the normative question of whether it deserves obedience remains fully open and contested — precisely the ground later lessons on natural law and positivism fight over.

testPool.prompt: A commentator argues: 'The rule requiring seatbelts is law only because Parliament enacted it and courts enforce it — nothing about its moral merit is relevant to whether it counts as law.' A second commentator replies: 'That may describe how the system works, but it says nothing about whether people are morally free to disregard the rule if they think it paternalistic.' Analyse what kind of disagreement, if any, exists between the two commentators.
factsToOrder: The first commentator's claim rests on enactment and enforcement by institutions
The first commentator explicitly sets moral merit aside
The second commentator does not deny the first commentator's account of validity
The second commentator instead raises a separate question about moral freedom to disregard the rule

scaffolds.support: Full model answer shown, mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule given; student applies it to the facts and writes the conclusion
No scaffold; student writes the full analysis unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether the two commentators are actually disagreeing about the same question.
modelAnswer.rule: A descriptive claim about what makes a rule legally valid (enactment and enforcement) is a different kind of claim from a normative claim about whether that valid rule deserves obedience or may be morally disregarded; the two can both be true at once without contradiction.
modelAnswer.application: The first commentator is making a descriptive claim about the source of the seatbelt rule's legal validity, and expressly excludes moral merit from that inquiry. The second commentator does not contest that account of validity at all — they accept it and move to a separate, normative question about whether a valid rule commands moral compliance. Because the two are answering different questions, there is no real contradiction between them, only a difference in what each is asking.
modelAnswer.conclusion: The two commentators are not disagreeing about the same question — the first is speaking descriptively about validity, the second normatively about obedience — so no genuine contradiction has been shown.

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that every theory covered in this module answers Hart's three recurring puzzles (obligation, the law/morality connection, and the nature of rules) in exactly the same way?
sliderLabels: Confident — they give genuinely rival answers
testPool.correctPosition: Confident — they give genuinely rival answers
testPool.explanation: The theories in this module give substantively different, carefully argued answers to these puzzles — that rivalry is the reason the module exists, and why it is built to test accurate statement of each position rather than agreement with any one of them.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson's test items is collapsing the descriptive and normative questions into one — treating 'this is validly enacted law' and 'this deserves to be obeyed' as if answering one automatically answers the other. Keeping them separate is the single skill every later lesson in this module assumes you already have.
